docs.title: Traffic Monitor docs
docs.text:
Traffic Monitor is open source software that turns a Raspberry Pi 5 with a camera and a Doppler radar into a roadway counter and speed monitor. It counts pedestrians, bicycles, and vehicles, measures vehicle speeds, and keeps the data on the device.

Be counted

Privacy is part of the design. Object detection runs on the device, the database records labels, speeds, and times rather than people, and nothing is sent to an outside server unless you set it up. Data and privacy lists what the device stores, including the short-lived snapshots and clips that Frigate keeps by default, and who on your network can see them.

Our mission is to democratize the power of AI tools to improve community safety and quality of life, through the ethical and transparent use of these capabilities.

docs.title: Choose a site and mount
docs.text:
Deployment covers where the device goes, how it's mounted, and the angle of the camera and radar to the roadway. The zones and location are set afterwards in First-time setup.

Danger

Follow the law. Comply with all applicable laws and local regulations when installing, mounting, and deploying a Traffic Monitor, particularly in public spaces. Unauthorized surveillance can lead to legal consequences and infringe privacy rights. Consult legal professionals or local authorities if you are unsure of the requirements. This guide is for educational purposes; you are responsible for complying with the law and for the consequences of deploying and using the device.

Mount the device only where you have permission, and don't attach it to utility poles without proper authorization.

docs.title: Mounting options
docs.text:
Choose a mount that lets you make fine adjustments, because the radar's angle and position need tuning on site.

The open source, 3D-printed enclosure has several mounting methods built in, depending on the variant:

  • 1/4"-20 screw insert on the bottom and back, for camera and trail-camera mounting hardware
  • VESA-compatible holes (75 and 100 mm)
  • Arca-Swiss-compatible quick-release plate on the bottom, for tripods
  • Strap slots on the back, for posts, poles, and trees
  • Safety tether hole for a carabiner and strap
Back: VESA holes, 1/4"-20 screw insert, strap slots, and safety tether hole (lower left) Bottom: Arca-Swiss quick-release plate and 1/4"-20 screw insert

docs.title: Temporary deployments
docs.text:
For counts over a few hours, such as an event or a point-in-time study, mount the device at or above head height with an unobstructed view of the roadway. A sturdy tripod and a compact portable power station work well.

On a 16-foot telescoping tripod, counting event participants Recording manual confirmation counts, with the device on a camera tripod and a portable power station

docs.title: Permanent deployments
docs.text:
Warning

Work safely. Use proper safety equipment and ladder practice. Make sure the device is securely mounted, all fasteners are tight, the safety tether is in place, and the mount is stable. Failure to do so can cause injury or property damage.

Long-term deployments work anywhere the camera has a good view of the roadway and the radar can be aimed along it: garage roofs, a wood post in a cement-filled bucket, a stone pillar. Keep the device out of reach and clear of anything that might grow or be parked in front of it.

Long-term deployments, with permission, on a private rooftop and a gate entrance

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Mount the device above the roadway and out of reach, about 10 to 12 feet up, for the best view and the least tampering.
  • Choose a clear view of the road. Objects are still tracked when they pass briefly behind a tree or lamp post.
  • Keep the radar off parking spots and other places where vehicles stop, because stationary vehicles get in the way of its readings.
  • The camera detects objects anywhere in its field of view, so frame the whole stretch of road you care about.
  • Think about which zones your use case needs, and whether the view lets you draw them.

docs.title: Sample deployments
docs.text: Quiet road, monitoring downhill movement Busy business district, nearly head-on movement on a wide road Busy business district, side-on view focused on a pedestrian and bike crosswalk Neighborhood greenway, an ideal spot to count bikes, pedestrians, and cars Greenway mounting spot, facing south Greenway mounting spot, facing north

docs.title: Camera considerations
docs.text:
The camera detects objects anywhere in the frame, so cover the whole area of interest even if the roadway isn't centered. An unobstructed view gives the best results.

Detections can happen anywhere in the camera's field of view

docs.title: Radar considerations
docs.text:
The radar has a narrower field of view than the camera and measures speed accurately only at a shallow angle to the direction of travel.

  • Aim the device so that traffic moves toward or away from it at 45 degrees or less. The OmniPreSense field-of-view calculator shows how the angle affects the reading.
  • The radar labels movement inbound (toward the device) and outbound (away from it), and the camera uses the same words. Place the device so those directions make sense for your roadway, for example inbound for downhill traffic.
  • To find the radar's coverage, have someone hold the radar outside the case and watch the red and blue LEDs on its front as people and vehicles pass. Where the LEDs blink is where to draw zone_radar.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text: Plug the device in. It starts by itself, and the green LED on the Raspberry Pi shows it has power. Continue with First-time setup.

docs.title: 1. Get a Traffic Monitor
docs.text:
• Build your own

    Buy the hardware, assemble it, and install the software. The software is open source and the parts are sold at retail.

  • Start with a pre-built unit

    The software is installed. Skip to step 2, and ask your provider how the unit connects to your network.

docs.title: 2. Deploy it
docs.text: The device needs a clear view of the roadway, and the radar needs a shallow angle to the direction of travel. Choose a site and mount covers both, for temporary and permanent deployments.

docs.title: 3. Set it up
docs.text: Power it on and follow First-time setup: open the home page, turn on detection, adjust the zones to your roadway, and record the device's location. This takes about half an hour.

docs.title: 4. Use the data
docs.text:
The device counts around the clock and starts again by itself after a power cut. Watch the Monitoring dashboard, review detections in Frigate, export the data, or send it to ThingsBoard.

Some operators pair the device with a display that shows the day's counts. Share what you build in Show and tell or on the Zulip chat.

LED display showing daily counts from a Traffic Monitor

docs.title: First-time setup
docs.text:
Do these steps once the device is mounted and powered on, and again whenever you move it. You need a computer or phone on the same network, and an SSH client for step 4.

As installed, the camera and the first radar are turned on in the Traffic Monitor's settings, but Frigate's object detection is off. Nothing is counted until you turn it on in step 2.

docs.title: 1. Open the home page
docs.text: Open http://<device>/, where <device> is the hostname you set when imaging the card followed by .local, or the device's IP address. Home page and apps explains each link and how to find the address.

docs.title: 2. Turn on detection
docs.text:
1. Open Frigate from the home page.
  2. Go to Settings > Configuration editor.
  3. Under cameras: picam_h265: detect:, change enabled: false to enabled: true.
  4. Choose Save & Restart.

When Frigate is back, its live view draws a box around anything that moves past the camera.

docs.title: 3. Adjust the zones
docs.text:
The Traffic Monitor looks for four zones with fixed names. Frigate ships with all four drawn for a sample roadway; drag their corners to fit yours.

  1. In Frigate, go to Settings > Camera configuration > Masks / Zones.
  2. Edit each zone in the table below, then save. Frigate restarts.
Zone Draw it over Used for zone_capture The whole roadway you want to count, including sidewalks that are clearly in view Counting. An object is counted only if it passes through this zone. zone_near The half of zone_capture closest to the device Direction zone_far The half of zone_capture farthest from the device Direction. An object that enters zone_near and then zone_far is moving outbound, away from the device; the reverse is inbound. zone_radar The part of the road the radar covers accurately, roughly a rectangle from curb to curb in the middle of the frame. Skip it if the device has no radar. Speed statistics. Any object that enters a zone gets a speed from the radar, but the dashboards' speed statistics use only objects that passed through this zone. Radar considerations shows how to find the radar's coverage. The four zones drawn over a residential street

Zones you draw for your own analysis, such as a stop-sign zone or a crosswalk, can have any other name. Ideas and use cases has examples.

docs.title: 4. Record the location and sensors
docs.text:
The device records its location with every event, so set it before you collect data. Connect over SSH and open the Traffic Monitor settings file:

sudo nano /opt/traffic-monitor/node-red-tm/config/config.yml
  1. Under deployment, enter the latitude and longitude from any map service, and the compass direction the camera faces as n, s, e, w, ne, nw, se, or sw.
  2. Under sensors, check that the entries match the hardware. A device with the Pi camera and one radar needs no change. A device without a radar needs enabled: false under TM_RADAR_SERIAL_PORT_00.
deployment:
    lat: 45.5225
    lon: -122.6919
    bearing: n

sensors:
    cameras:
        picam_h265:
            enabled: true
            camera_radar: TM_RADAR_SERIAL_PORT_00
    radars:
        TM_RADAR_SERIAL_PORT_00:
            enabled: true

Save with Ctrl+O and leave nano with Ctrl+X. The Traffic Monitor reads the file again as soon as you save it, so no restart is needed. A change that doesn't take effect usually means a YAML error, such as a wrong indent.

config.yml settings describes every setting in this file, including the optional ThingsBoard upload.

docs.title: 5. Check the counts
docs.text:
Open Dashboard from the home page and choose Monitoring in the sidebar. Monitoring shows a count a few seconds after each object passes through zone_capture, and speed statistics for objects that also passed through zone_radar. Today's counts start at 04:00 local time, so between midnight and 04:00 they're empty.

No counts?

Work down the list:

  1. Frigate shows no boxes around moving objects. Detection is off (step 2), or the camera is off: in the configuration editor, cameras: picam_h265: needs enabled: true. If the live view is black, open Go2RTC Feeds from the home page to check that the camera itself streams.
  2. Frigate detects objects, but the dashboard stays at zero. The objects aren't passing through zone_capture (step 3), or the camera is off in the Traffic Monitor's settings: sensors: cameras: picam_h265: needs enabled: true, and the name must match Frigate's camera name. If your edits don't take effect, check the file for a YAML error.
  3. Counts but no speeds. The radar must be enabled: true and named in the camera's camera_radar, zone_radar must cover the road, and the radar must have been plugged in when the software was installed. If you added it later, rerun bash traffic-monitor/script/tmsetup.sh -t node-red-tm.
  4. Still nothing. Look at the logs in System administration, then ask in the chat.

docs.title: Install the software
docs.text: The Traffic Monitor runs on a Raspberry Pi 5 with Raspberry Pi OS Lite (64-bit). One installer script sets up the operating system, detects the radars and the AI accelerator, builds the containers on the device, and reboots when it needs to.

docs.title: Prepare the card
docs.text:
1. Open Raspberry Pi Imager on your computer, with the microSD card in a card reader.
  2. Choose Raspberry Pi OS (other) > Raspberry Pi OS Lite (64-bit). The full desktop image works but installs software the Traffic Monitor doesn't use.
  3. In OS customization, set a hostname, a username and password, your Wi-Fi network, and turn on SSH. The hostname becomes the device's address on your network: http://<hostname>.local/.
  4. Write the card, put it in the Raspberry Pi, and power it on. The first boot takes a few minutes.

docs.title: Install on the device
docs.text:
The device needs an internet connection during the install. Afterwards it runs offline.

Connect over SSH with the username and hostname you chose:

ssh <username>@<hostname>.local

Then download the repository and run the installer:

sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y git
git clone https://github.com/glossyio/traffic-monitor
bash traffic-monitor/script/tmsetup.sh

The installer asks for your password when it needs administrator rights. A first install takes 30 minutes or more. Building Frigate's container image compiles ffmpeg on the device, which alone takes about 20 minutes with little output, so leave it running.

Near the end, the installer asks to reboot. A first install always needs the reboot, with or without an AI accelerator, because it changes the Raspberry Pi's boot settings for the camera and any accelerator it found. The services start after the reboot. After it, open http://<hostname>.local/ and continue with First-time setup.

The installer's flags, such as a different install folder or time zone, are listed in Installer options.

docs.title: Install from another computer
docs.text:
The same script can install or update one or more devices over SSH from a Linux or Mac computer. Each device needs Raspberry Pi OS, a network connection, and an address you can reach.

git clone https://github.com/glossyio/traffic-monitor
bash traffic-monitor/script/tmsetup.sh -H <address>[,<address>] -l <username> -k -K
Flag Meaning -H The devices' hostnames or IP addresses, separated by commas -l The username you set when imaging the cards. It must be the same on every device. -k Ask for the SSH password -K Ask for the password for administrator rights. Raspberry Pi OS requires it.

Remote devices reboot by themselves when the install needs it.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
1. Choose a site and mount the device.
  2. First-time setup: turn on detection, adjust the zones, and record the location.

docs.title: description: Add the Enviro+ air quality sensor to a Traffic Monitor: hardware, the sensor software, and the settings that connect it.
Air quality sensor
docs.text:
The optional air quality sensor measures gases, particulate matter, temperature, pressure, humidity, and light. Readings go into the device's database every five minutes and appear on the legacy dashboard.

We make no warranty on the accuracy of the sensor or its data. If you have an environmental science background, we'd welcome your help.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: The Pimoroni Enviro+ board with the Plantower PMS5003 particulate matter sensor, connected to the Raspberry Pi's GPIO header with a ribbon cable. The assembly steps show where the sensor sits in the enclosure. Pimoroni's getting started guide covers the board itself.

docs.title: Sensor software
docs.text:
The sensor is read by greendormer/enviroplus-monitor, a Python service that runs on the Raspberry Pi and publishes readings to the device's MQTT broker. Install it following that repository's instructions, then set these keys in its config.json (key reference):

Key Value Why enable_send_data_to_homemanager true Publish readings over MQTT mqtt_broker_name "localhost" The Traffic Monitor's broker, on port 1883 mqtt_username, mqtt_password The broker's login Needed once the broker has a login. See Connect from other devices. indoor_outdoor_function "Outdoor" Use the outdoor topic outdoor_mqtt_topic "aq/sensorname01/readings" The topic must start with aq/, and the middle part is the sensor's name in the Traffic Monitor's settings enable_display false The board's screen is inside the enclosure long_update_delay 300 Seconds between readings

Set the location keys for your site as well. The software uses them to calibrate the pressure and gas readings for altitude, and to work out sunrise and sunset:

{
    "altitude": 49,
    "city_name": "Portland",
    "time_zone": "America/Los_Angeles",
    "custom_locations": [
        "Portland, United States of America, America/Los_Angeles, 45.52, -122.681944"
    ]
}

docs.title: Turn the sensor on in the Traffic Monitor
docs.text:
In /opt/traffic-monitor/node-red-tm/config/config.yml, under sensors: airquality_monitors:, set the sensor's entry to enabled: true. The entry's name must match the middle part of the MQTT topic:

sensors:
    airquality_monitors:
        sensorname01:
            enabled: true

The change takes effect when you save the file. Readings from a sensor that isn't enabled are dropped.

docs.title: What to expect
docs.text:
• The first readings arrive after the sensor's stabilization period, five minutes by default (startup_stabilisation_time in config.json).
  • The gas readings are reported as uncalibrated for the first 100 minutes, while the gas sensor warms up.
  • Readings show in the Air Quality section of the legacy dashboard at http://<device>/ui/, and are stored in the airquality table. Air quality describes the payload and the columns.
  • The Raspberry Pi and the AI accelerator give off heat. The enclosure separates the sensor from them, but temperature and humidity may still read high.

docs.title: Plate Recognizer
docs.text:
Plate Recognizer is an optional add-on built on a commercial product from Plate Recognizer, a company the Traffic Monitor project isn't affiliated with. It's off unless you install it. The add-on runs the company's on-device license plate reader in a container next to Frigate. For each car event from a camera you choose that passed through zone_radar, it reads the plate from Frigate's snapshot and stores the plate number, region, and vehicle make, model, and color.

Frigate has its own license plate recognition, which the Traffic Monitor doesn't turn on.

Danger

Plates identify people. With this add-on on, the database is no longer de-identified: the plate_recognizer table holds plate numbers. Keep the database on the device, don't share it, and make sure your use complies with local law. See Data and privacy.

You need a Plate Recognizer account with an on-premise (SDK) license, which gives you an API token and a license key.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
1. Run the installer with the add-on turned on:

    bash traffic-monitor/script/tmsetup.sh -C plate_recognizer

  2. Put your credentials in /opt/traffic-monitor/plate-recognizer/plate-recognizer.env:

    Variable Value TOKEN Your Plate Recognizer API token LICENSE_KEY Your on-premise license key WORKERS Parallel readers. 2 suits a Raspberry Pi 5.

  3. Add the token and the add-on's address to /opt/traffic-monitor/node-red-tm/config/config.yml, and turn the add-on on for each camera whose events should be read:

    sensors:
    cameras:
        picam_h265:
            enabled: true
            plate_recognizer: true

addons:
    plate_recognizer:
        token: <your API token>
        url: http://plate-recognizer:8080

  4. Restart the add-on so it reads its env file, and again whenever you change that file:

    sudo systemctl restart plate-recognizer.service

    Node-RED picks up config.yml as soon as you save it, so it needs no restart.

Frigate's snapshots must stay on, which they are by default; the reader works from them.

docs.title: Data
docs.text:
Each read goes into the plate_recognizer table, keyed by the event it belongs to.

Column Type Meaning event_id TEXT, primary key The id of the event filename TEXT The snapshot that was read timestamp TEXT The event's frame_time, when Frigate took the best frame of the car camera_id TEXT Always picam_h264, whichever camera the event came from processing_time REAL Milliseconds the read took plate_type TEXT Plate category, if the reader reports one plate_score REAL Confidence that a plate was found, 0 to 1 plate_xmin, plate_ymin, plate_xmax, plate_ymax INTEGER The plate's box in the snapshot, in pixels plate_value TEXT The plate number plate_value_score REAL Confidence in the plate number, 0 to 1 plate_region_value TEXT The issuing region, such as us-or. The reader looks only for us, us-or, and us-wa plates. plate_region_score REAL Confidence in the region, 0 to 1 vehicle_type TEXT Vehicle category, such as Sedan vehicle_score REAL Confidence in the vehicle, 0 to 1 vehicle_xmin, vehicle_ymin, vehicle_xmax, vehicle_ymax INTEGER The vehicle's box in the snapshot, in pixels vehicle_make, vehicle_model TEXT Make and model vehicle_make_model_score REAL Confidence in make and model, 0 to 1 vehicle_orientation TEXT Front, Rear, or similar vehicle_orientation_score REAL Confidence in the orientation, 0 to 1 vehicle_color TEXT Color vehicle_color_score REAL Confidence in the color, 0 to 1 json_payload TEXT The reader's full JSON response

docs.title: Build your own
docs.text:
A Traffic Monitor is a Raspberry Pi 5, a camera, an optional radar and AI accelerator, and a weather-resistant enclosure. Building one takes an afternoon.

  1. Hardware: the parts list, with the options that have been tested.
  2. Assembly: fitting the parts into the 3D-printed enclosure.
  3. Install the software: image the microSD card and run the installer.
  4. Update the software: when a new release comes out.

Then continue with Choose a site and mount and First-time setup.

docs.title: description: The parts for a Traffic Monitor: Raspberry Pi 5, camera, AI accelerator, radar, enclosure, power, and the optional air quality sensor.
Hardware
docs.text:
The core parts are the Raspberry Pi 5, a microSD card, a camera, and an AI accelerator. A radar adds accurate speeds, and an air quality sensor adds environmental readings. You can swap parts, but the docs and the default settings assume the parts below.

What each combination gives you:

  1. Camera and AI accelerator: object detection and counts. The lowest cost.
  2. Add a radar for speeds and the direction of travel. Without a radar, events have no speed or direction.
  3. Add an air quality sensor for gases, particulate matter, temperature, pressure, humidity, and light.
  4. Add cameras to watch more directions with the same accelerator. The software supports several cameras and up to four radars, paired in any pattern. See Cameras.

docs.title: Parts list
docs.text:
We are not affiliated with the stores or companies linked here. These are parts contributors have used or tested; if you've tested others, post in the discussions.

  • Computer: Raspberry Pi 5, 4 GB or 8 GB
    • Power: the official 27 W USB-C power supply
    • Cooling: the Raspberry Pi active cooler
  • Storage: a microSD card of 32 GB or more, such as the Raspberry Pi SD card or the SanDisk Extreme Pro
  • Camera: Raspberry Pi Camera Module 3, wide angle, plus a Raspberry Pi 5 camera cable
  • AI accelerator: see AI accelerator
  • Radar (recommended): OmniPreSense OPS243-A
  • Enclosure: see Enclosure
  • Air quality sensor (optional): Enviro+ with the PMS5003 particulate matter sensor and a male-to-female GPIO ribbon cable
  • Screws: assorted M3 for the boards and enclosure, M2.5×10 mm for the Raspberry Pi

docs.title: Computer
docs.text:
The Raspberry Pi 5 with 4 GB of memory runs the standard setup. Choose 8 GB if you plan to add sensors or other applications. Add the active cooler; it's inexpensive and prevents throttling on hot days.

Warning

The Raspberry Pi 4 and earlier can't supply enough power over USB for the accelerator and the radar together, which causes resets and dropped readings. Some people have run object detection alone on older models.

docs.title: Storage
docs.text: A good microSD card of 32 GB or more holds the system and the database. Both the Raspberry Pi SD card and the SanDisk Extreme Pro have been tested. An NVMe (M.2) drive is faster and more durable, and some M.2 HATs hold both a drive and a Coral accelerator.

docs.title: Power
docs.text:
The Raspberry Pi 5 needs a 27 W supply (5 V at 5 A). A weaker supply, such as an older Raspberry Pi adapter, causes resets and throttling. The device itself draws 6 to 14 W while detecting, and every part is powered from the Raspberry Pi.

  • Mains: the official 27 W USB-C power supply.
  • Power over Ethernet: a PoE HAT such as the Waveshare PoE HAT (F) or Waveshare PoE M.2 HAT+, with a PoE+ source such as the Raspberry Pi PoE+ injector.
  • Battery for about a day: a portable power station such as a Jackery Explorer 300, with the official power supply plugged into it. A 300 Wh station lasts about a day.
Longer off-grid use: custom battery and solar

Battery. Use a 12 V or 24 V LiFePO₄ battery and a buck converter that steps it down to 5 V at 5 A. Size the battery from the device's draw of about 13 W: a 12 V, 10 Ah battery (120 Wh) lasts about 9 hours, and 24 hours needs 13 × 24 = 312 Wh, a 12 V battery of about 30 Ah.

Solar. Add a photovoltaic panel and a charge controller to the battery setup. Size the panel for the worst month:

  1. Look up your daily solar potential. Portland, Oregon, gets about 7.15 kWh/day in summer and 1.42 kWh/day in winter per kW of panel.
  2. Multiply by the panel size. A 100 W panel in a Portland winter produces about 1.42 × 0.1 = 142 Wh per day.
  3. Allow for the controller. A PWM controller passes about 80%, so 142 × 0.8 = 113 Wh per day.
  4. Compare with the 312 Wh the device uses per day. A 100 W panel isn't enough; a Portland winter needs about 300 W of panel.

Real output depends on panel angle, cloud, shade from trees, and snow. This setup is a prototype, not a tested product.

docs.title: Cameras
docs.text:
The Raspberry Pi Camera Module 3 in its wide-angle version is the tested camera. It needs the Raspberry Pi 5 camera cable, sold separately. The Raspberry Pi Global Shutter camera has been tested too, for faster motion or a custom lens, with the same cable. It needs camera stream settings that match its sensor, because the defaults are for Camera Module 3. They're in /var/lib/go2rtc/go2rtc.yaml, which every update replaces, so redo them after updating.

The Raspberry Pi 5 has two camera connectors, so it can take two Raspberry Pi cameras. Network cameras also work; see Frigate's camera recommendations. Choose one that streams H.265 (HEVC), which the Raspberry Pi 5 decodes in hardware. H.264 works with software decoding but costs CPU, so keep to one or two such cameras.

docs.title: AI accelerator
docs.text:
An AI accelerator runs the object detection model at over 100 frames per second with a few milliseconds per inference, enough for several cameras. Without one, Frigate detects on the CPU, which is slower and misses more objects on a busy road, so an accelerator is recommended for any deployment with a camera.

  1. Recommended: Raspberry Pi AI HAT+ with the Hailo-8 or Hailo-8L.
  2. Older: Coral USB Accelerator. It has become expensive and hard to find.
  3. Older: Coral M.2 Accelerator B+M key (not the A+E key) on the Raspberry Pi M.2 HAT+.

Frigate's supported detectors lists other options. The installer detects the Coral and Hailo accelerators and configures Frigate for whichever it finds.

docs.title: Radar
docs.text: The OmniPreSense OPS243-A Doppler radar measures speed and direction up to about 100 m away and is certified with the same tests as law-enforcement speed radars. It connects over USB.

docs.title: Air quality sensor
docs.text: The Enviro+ board with the PMS5003 particulate matter sensor measures gases, particulates, temperature, pressure, humidity, and light. It plugs into the Raspberry Pi's GPIO header through a male-to-female ribbon cable, which reaches the sensor's place in the enclosure. Air quality sensor covers the software.

docs.title: Enclosure
docs.text:
• Print it. The 3D-printable enclosure is open source at greendormer/tm-enclosure-3d, with a parts list.

  • Adapt a junction box. A waterproof electrical box of about 9 × 7 × 4 inches, such as the TICONN IP67 ABS enclosure, holds the parts, the camera, and the radar with some modification.

docs.title: Update the software
docs.text: An update reruns the installer from a newer copy of the repository. Your data and your settings stay; the containers are rebuilt.

docs.title: Before you update
docs.text:
• Read the release notes. A release that needs a fresh image says so.
  • Download a copy of the database from the Data export page.
  • Make sure the device has an internet connection. The update downloads packages and rebuilds the container images. Rebuilding Frigate's image compiles ffmpeg on the device, which can take about 20 minutes.

docs.title: Update
docs.text:
Connect to the device over SSH, then update the clone you installed from and rerun the whole installer:

cd traffic-monitor
git pull
bash script/tmsetup.sh

Run the whole installer rather than a single tag, because one version's changes can span several components.

Restart when the installer asks. When the services come back, the Node-RED service applies any database schema changes before it opens the database. Schema versions describes the copy it saves first.

The installer printed tm-control migrate: WARNING

A camera's input path in Frigate's configuration reads a stream on port 8554 without a login. If that path points at this device, for example by its IP address, add {FRIGATE_GO2RTC_RTSP_USER}:{FRIGATE_GO2RTC_RTSP_PASSWORD}@ before the host in Frigate's configuration editor. The higher-resolution stream section shows a complete path. If it points at another device, leave it as it is. To find the warning later:

grep 'tm-control migrate: WARNING' ~/tmsetup-*.log

A Frigate configuration from a backup may lack the camera stream login. After you restore one, run bash script/tmsetup.sh -t frigate to add it.

Port 1883 accepts MQTT connections only from the device itself unless the broker has a login. If a display board, Home Assistant, or another device on your network reads MQTT from this device, give the broker a login and give it to that device; see Connect from other devices.

Open http://<device>/ and check the Monitoring dashboard for new counts.

To update several devices from your computer, use the remote form of the installer described in Install the software.

docs.title: What an update changes
docs.text:
An update replaces the container images, service units, Node-RED flows, and the reverse proxy configuration. It keeps your settings files, the database, and Frigate's recordings. With -f, it also replaces the settings files with fresh copies from the templates and keeps each old file beside the new one with a timestamp. What -f replaces lists the files.

Use -f when a release changes the settings files and you want the new template. Afterwards, turn Frigate's detection back on and redo your settings from the timestamped copies: location and sensors in config.yml, and zones in Frigate. First-time setup walks through each.

Node-RED flow changes made in the editor on the device are replaced on every update. Commit them to the repository instead; see Dev environment.

docs.title: Update one component
docs.text:
Each installer tag reruns one component, plus anything that has to change with it; see Tags. For example, after plugging in a radar:

bash script/tmsetup.sh -t node-red-tm

Installer options lists the tags and flags.

docs.title: description: The variables in node-red-tm.env: radar serial ports, database path, MQTT broker, and the values the installer fills in.
node-red-tm.env settings
docs.text:
/opt/traffic-monitor/node-red-tm/node-red-tm.env holds the environment the Node-RED container starts with. The installer writes it from this template on the first install and leaves it alone afterwards, unless you run the installer with -f. Most devices never need it edited.

After editing it, restart the service:

sudo systemctl restart node-red-tm.service

After changing the MQTT broker login

A restart or reboot isn't enough after you change TM_MQTT_BROKER_USERNAME or TM_MQTT_BROKER_PASSWORD. Run the installer instead, so Frigate gets the same login and port 1883 opens or closes to match:

bash traffic-monitor/script/tmsetup.sh -t node-red-tm

Otherwise the broker refuses Frigate's connection, and no events are recorded.

Variable Default Meaning TM_VERSION the installed release The Traffic Monitor version, shown on the dashboards and sent with telemetry. The installer sets it; don't edit it. TM_RPI_SN the Raspberry Pi's serial number Identifies the device in ThingsBoard, and fills deviceName in deployment records. Set by the installer. TM_HOSTNAME the device's hostname at install Prefix for the file names of data exports. Set by the installer. NODE_RED_CREDENTIAL_SECRET myNodeRED1234 Encrypts the credentials saved in the Node-RED editor. Leave it as it is: every installer run copies in the repository's credentials file, which is encrypted with this default, so a changed value leaves Node-RED unable to read it. TM_DATABASE_PATH_TMDB /db/tmdb.sqlite The database, as seen inside the container. On the device it's /opt/traffic-monitor/node-red-tm/db/tmdb.sqlite. Leave it; schema migrations and downloads expect this path. TM_MQTT_BROKER_HOST localhost The MQTT broker that Node-RED hosts. Frigate and the air quality sensor publish to it. See MQTT and ThingsBoard. TM_MQTT_BROKER_PORT 1883 The broker's port. TM_MQTT_BROKER_USERNAME empty The broker's login username. When it and the password are both set, the broker requires the login from every client, and port 1883 opens to the network. Letters, digits, ., _, and - only, with no quotes and no comment after the value. See Connect from other devices. TM_MQTT_BROKER_PASSWORD empty The broker's login password, with the same rules as the username. TM_RADAR_SERIAL_PORT_00 to TM_RADAR_SERIAL_PORT_03 /dev/ttyACM0 to /dev/ttyACM3 The serial port of each radar. The variable's name is the radar's name in config.yml. The installer passes only the ports that exist at install time into the container, so after plugging in a radar rerun bash traffic-monitor/script/tmsetup.sh -t node-red-tm.

docs.title: Tune object detection
docs.text:
Frigate does the object detection. How well it works depends on the mounting height and angle, the camera, and the weather, so expect to adjust it for each site. The Traffic Monitor is not affiliated with the Frigate project.

The Traffic Monitor's default Frigate config is tuned for roadways seen from an oblique angle, with a side view of objects as they pass. Everything in it can be changed in Frigate's own UI, at Settings > Configuration editor. Frigate's configuration reference explains every setting.

docs.title: See what Frigate sees
docs.text:
Go to Settings > Debug to watch detections live with their scores, and the motion regions Frigate is checking. Explore lists past detections with their snapshots, which is the quickest way to find missed bikes or a tree that's being called a person.

The debug view shows how detection is performing

docs.title: Object filters
docs.text:
Frigate tracks bicycle, person, car, bus, motorcycle, and dog by default. Each object type has two scores in the objects: filters: section of the config:

  • min_score is the score needed to start tracking an object.
  • threshold is the average score an object needs, over the time it's tracked, to count as a real detection.

The defaults set bicycle low, so most kinds of bike are detected, and motorcycle high, so a large e-bike isn't called a motorcycle. If you see false positives for a type, raise its threshold; if you miss objects, lower it. Frigate's object filters page describes these and the size and shape filters.

docs.title: Masks
docs.text:
Go to Settings > Camera configuration > Masks / Zones.

  • A motion mask stops motion in an area, such as swaying branches or a timestamp overlay, from triggering detection.
  • An object mask ignores detections of one object type in an area, such as a parked car that's detected every time the light changes.

Warning

Use masks sparingly. Over-masking makes objects harder to track. A motion mask isn't the tool for cutting false positives; adjust the object filters first.

Frigate's masks page has the details.

docs.title: Higher-resolution stream
docs.text:
The Pi camera is set up to produce two streams. Frigate uses picam_h265_detect at 1536×864 by default, which gives the best balance of detail and load. A second stream, picam_h265_detect_hr, runs at 2304×1296 for cases where objects are small in the frame.

To switch, change two things in the configuration editor under cameras: picam_h265:: the input path to rtsp://{FRIGATE_GO2RTC_RTSP_USER}:{FRIGATE_GO2RTC_RTSP_PASSWORD}@host.containers.internal:8554/picam_h265_detect_hr, and detect: width: 2304 with height: 1296. Frigate fills in the {…} values from frigate.env. Then redraw the zones for the new frame size. The higher resolution costs CPU and may lower the frame rate on a busy road.

docs.title: Recordings and snapshots
docs.text:
By default, Frigate keeps a cropped snapshot of each detection and a recording of each alert and detection for about an hour, so you can check what was detected. The record: and snapshots: sections control this: set enabled: false to keep nothing, or raise retain: days to keep more. Data and privacy describes what the device stores.

Frigate can also publish a cropped snapshot of each detected object on the device's MQTT broker. The Traffic Monitor doesn't use these snapshots, so new installs turn them off with mqtt: enabled: false under cameras: picam_h265:. On an older install, add those lines in the configuration editor. Frigate keeps publishing the events the Traffic Monitor counts.

cameras:
  picam_h265:
    mqtt:
      enabled: false

docs.title: Better models
docs.text: Frigate+ offers paid models fine-tuned on your own snapshots, which can raise accuracy for a difficult site.

docs.title: config.yml settings
docs.text:
The Traffic Monitor's own settings live in /opt/traffic-monitor/node-red-tm/config/config.yml on the device. The installer writes it from this template on the first install and leaves it alone afterwards, unless you run the installer with -f.

The Traffic Monitor reads the file again whenever you save it, so changes take effect without a restart. If the file has a YAML error, it keeps the previous settings until the service restarts, and after a restart it has no settings at all until you fix the file.

Keep the four top-level sections (thingsboard, deployment, sensors, time) in the file. The Default column below shows the values the template writes. A setting that's missing from the file behaves differently in a few cases:

  • A camera or radar without enabled is off.
  • A radar without opt_api_commands_array gets no extra commands.
  • ThingsBoard without host stays off.
  • A deployment without lat or lon isn't recorded, so leave the keys in place even when they're empty.
  • A camera whose camera_radar names a radar that isn't in the file records no events. On a device without a radar, remove camera_radar or keep the radar's entry with enabled: false.

docs.title: thingsboard
docs.text:
Uploads events, readings, and device telemetry to a ThingsBoard server. See MQTT and ThingsBoard.

Required when enabled. protocol http or https https How to reach the server. port number none Set it only if the server isn't on the standard port for the protocol. access_token text empty The device's access token from ThingsBoard. This is the one secret in the file.

docs.text:
Where the device is. Every event and reading is stored with a deployment id that points at these values, so set them before you collect data and update them when you move the device.

A deployment: block with the same three settings under any sensor overrides these for that sensor, for a device whose cameras face different ways.

docs.title: Air quality
docs.text: The optional air quality sensor publishes a reading over MQTT every five minutes. The Traffic Monitor stores each reading as a row in the airquality table.

docs.text:
The sensor software publishes to aq/<sensor>/readings, where <sensor> is the sensor's name in config.yml. Readings are dropped unless that sensor is enabled there.

{
    "gas_calibrated": false,
    "bar": [1009.44, "0"],
    "hum": [28.7, "2"],
    "pm025": 0,
    "pm10": 0,
    "pm01": 0,
    "dew": 2.1,
    "temp": 21,
    "temp_min": 20.9,
    "temp_max": 21.1,
    "gas_red": 4.2,
    "gas_oxi": 0.15,
    "gas_nh3": 0.69,
    "lux": 1.2,
    "proximity": 255,
    "lux_raw": 1.16185,
    "temp_raw": 28.68982029794099,
    "bar_raw": 1003.7122773175154,
    "hum_raw": 18.31337919009301,
    "gas_red_raw": 140805,

}

Only the value is stored. temp_min, temp_max, and the sensor software's Forecast object aren't stored. The sensor software's README explains how it compensates and calibrates the readings.

Treat the ppm values as relative; see the discussion in pimoroni/enviroplus-python #47 and #67. docs.title: Data and privacy
docs.text: The Traffic Monitor is a data collection tool. Everything it collects is processed and stored on the device, in open formats, so you own it and can share it.

docs.title: What the device stores
docs.text: Where What How long /opt/traffic-monitor/node-red-tm/db/tmdb.sqlite The database: events, radar readings, air quality readings, the device's deployment history, and operator comments Until you delete it /opt/traffic-monitor/frigate/storage/ Frigate's cropped snapshots of each detection, and recordings of alerts and detections About an hour, by default Your ThingsBoard server A copy of the data above, plus system metrics If you turn on the ThingsBoard upload

docs.title: Privacy
docs.text:
We believe in open data: anonymized data is a public good and the basis of useful research. The database is designed to be shareable. With the default settings it is de-identified: it records what passed (a label), when, how fast, and through which zones, and never an image or a plate number.

Images do exist on the device, briefly. Frigate keeps snapshots and short clips for about an hour so you can check what it detected. To keep none, turn off recordings and snapshots as described in Tune object detection. To keep them longer, raise the retention there, and treat the device as holding images of people.

By default, the device sends no images or video anywhere. Everything is processed on the device, and tmdb.sqlite holds only metadata. Anyone on the device's network can still see images, though. The live view and the recordings have no login; Home page and apps shows which apps ask for one. Frigate can also publish a snapshot of each detected object on the device's MQTT broker. New installs turn those snapshots off, and they stay on the device unless you give the broker a login, which opens it to your network. Tune object detection shows the setting.

The database stops being de-identified if you:

  • Install the Plate Recognizer add-on. Plate numbers go into the plate_recognizer table. Don't share a database from a device that has ever had the add-on on.
  • Turn on Frigate features that add identifying sub-labels or attributes to events, such as face recognition or license plate recognition.
  • Write identifying details into operator comments.

For an area the camera shouldn't see at all, such as a window or a yard, aim the camera so the area is out of frame. A motion mask only stops motion there from starting a detection; the area still shows in the live view and in recordings.

Other software on the device, such as Frigate and the air quality sensor's service, keeps its own working data under its own retention rules.

The radar tables are described on their own page. The two tables below have no other page.

Every other table's deployment_id column holds the id of one of these rows, so you can tell where a reading was taken after the device has moved. Free-text notes an operator adds on the Data export page, for example "threshold lowered to 0.4" or "road work on the north side", so that whoever analyzes the data later knows what changed and when.

docs.title: Schema versions
docs.text: The tables are defined by numbered migrations in the repository's container/node-red-tm/schema/ folder, and schema.sql there shows the whole current schema. Each time the Node-RED service starts, it applies any migrations the database doesn't have yet and records the schema version in the database. Before it does, it saves a copy of the database in /opt/traffic-monitor/node-red-tm/db/backup/ and keeps only the most recent copy. It makes no copy of a new database, or when the disk has less free space than about 1.2 times the database's size. It also makes none when the only migration to apply is the first, which only adds missing tables. You can read the version with PRAGMA user_version;.

docs.title: Getting the data
docs.text:
• Download the whole database, or a JSON export of events, radar readings, or air quality readings over a date range, from the Data export page.
  • Open the database with DB Browser for SQLite, or from code with any SQLite library, such as Python's built-in sqlite3.
  • Subscribe to today's counts over MQTT, or upload everything to ThingsBoard. See MQTT and ThingsBoard.
  • Review snapshots and clips in Frigate's Explore view at http://<device>/frigate/.

docs.title: description: The events table: one row per object the camera detected, with its label, times, zones, direction, and radar speed.
Events
docs.text: An event is one object that Frigate detected and tracked until it left the frame: a car, a person, a bicycle, and so on. When the camera has a radar, the Traffic Monitor adds the direction of travel and the speed, and it stores the result in the events table of the database.

docs.title: How an event is made
docs.text:
1. Frigate publishes a message on the device's MQTT topic frigate/events for each tracked object. When the object leaves the frame, the message has type: "end" and holds everything Frigate knows about it.
  2. The Traffic Monitor keeps the end message if the camera is enabled in config.yml and the object moved.
  3. If the object entered any zone and the camera has an enabled radar, it works out the direction and the speed, as described below, and adds radar to provenance when a speed was found.
  4. It writes the row, publishes today's counts on tm/events, and uploads the event to ThingsBoard if that is on. See MQTT and ThingsBoard.

First-time setup describes the four zones.

docs.title: Direction and speed
docs.text:
The zones give a direction when the object entered both zone_near and zone_far: zone_near then zone_far is outbound, and the reverse is inbound. The radar's readings come from the time the object was in view, with a two-second margin on each side. The radar reports a direction with each reading, and the speed is the median of the readings in the chosen direction.

Zones Radar readings direction_calc speed_calc A direction In that direction, or in both directions The zones' direction The median in that direction A direction Only in the other direction Empty Empty No direction In one direction only The radar's direction The median in that direction No direction In both directions Empty Empty A direction None The zones' direction Empty No direction None Empty Empty

An object that entered no zone, and every object on a camera without an enabled radar, has no direction and no speed.

docs.text:
Values that come straight from Frigate's message are marked Frigate. Frigate's MQTT page documents them in full.

docs.title: MQTT and ThingsBoard
docs.text: The MQTT broker is on by default and accepts connections only from the device itself. The ThingsBoard upload is off until you turn it on.

docs.title: MQTT
docs.text:
Node-RED hosts an MQTT broker on the device at port 1883. Frigate, the air quality sensor, and Node-RED connect to it on the device. Other devices on your network, such as Home Assistant or a display board that shows the day's counts, can connect once you give the broker a login; see Connect from other devices. Settings are in node-red-tm.env.

Topic Direction Contents frigate/events Frigate to the Traffic Monitor Frigate's event messages. The Traffic Monitor records the ones with type: "end" as events. frigate/<camera>/<object>/snapshot Frigate to subscribers A cropped JPEG of each detected object, which can show a person. Frigate publishes it only when the camera's mqtt setting is on, and new installs turn it off. The Traffic Monitor doesn't use it. See Tune object detection. aq/<sensor>/readings Air quality sensor to the Traffic Monitor One JSON reading. See Air quality. tm/events The Traffic Monitor to subscribers Today's cumulative counts, mainly for a display board. Published with QoS 1 and retained, so a new subscriber gets the latest counts at once. See below.

tm/event, without the s, is the per-event message inside Node-RED. Each recorded event carries it to the dashboards and to the ThingsBoard upload. It isn't published on the broker, so MQTT clients such as Home Assistant can't subscribe to it.

docs.title: tm/events
docs.text:
A JSON object with the same counts as Today's counts on the Monitoring dashboard: events that passed through zone_capture, for the camera selected on the legacy dashboard at http://<device>/ui/, in a day that starts at 04:00 local time.

Key Meaning car, person, bicycle, motorcycle, bus, dog, ... One key per object type that has been counted today, named as Frigate labels it bicycle_adj bicycle plus motorcycle. Present once a bicycle has been counted. person_adj person minus bicycle minus motorcycle: a pedestrian count, because every cyclist is also detected as a person. Scooter riders count as people. It can be negative, when more bicycles and motorcycles than people have been counted. Present once a person has been counted. event_latest The object type of the most recent counted event, such as car

To watch it from another computer:

mosquitto_sub -h <device> -u <username> -P <password> -t tm/events

docs.title: Connect from other devices
docs.text:
1. Give the broker a login:

    bash traffic-monitor/script/tmsetup.sh -t node-red-tm -C mqtt_lan

    This creates the username tm and a random password. To choose your own instead, set TM_MQTT_BROKER_USERNAME and TM_MQTT_BROKER_PASSWORD in /opt/traffic-monitor/node-red-tm/node-red-tm.env and run the command without -C mqtt_lan. Use only letters, digits, ., _, and -, with no quotes and no comment after the value on the same line; otherwise the installer stops with a message.

    The broker then requires the login from every client, the installer gives it to Frigate, and port 1883 opens to your network.

  2. Read the login:

    sudo grep ^TM_MQTT_BROKER_ /opt/traffic-monitor/node-red-tm/node-red-tm.env

  3. Give it to the air quality sensor and to each MQTT client.

  4. Check from another computer:

    mosquitto_sub -h <device> -u <username> -P <password> -t tm/events

  5. To change the login, edit the two values and run bash traffic-monitor/script/tmsetup.sh -t node-red-tm again. To remove it, leave both values blank and run the same command: the broker stops checking logins and port 1883 closes to the network.

Warning

The login crosses the network unencrypted, and anyone who has it can read every topic and publish false data. Open MQTT only on a network you trust.

docs.title: ThingsBoard
docs.text:
The device can upload its data to a ThingsBoard server, which gives you dashboards and storage for a fleet of devices. Turn it on in the thingsboard section of config.yml with the server's hostname and the device's access token. The device picks up the change when you save the file.

Once connected, the device sends over ThingsBoard's HTTP API:

  • Each event as telemetry, with ts set to the event's frame_time in milliseconds and values holding every column of the event.
  • Each radar and air quality reading as telemetry. Readings from the high-rate radar tables are batched to avoid hundreds of messages per vehicle.
  • The device's system metrics as telemetry, every five minutes.
  • The deployment location, radar information, and the Traffic Monitor settings as device attributes.

docs.title: Config backup
docs.text: With ThingsBoard connected, the Backup & Restore section of the legacy dashboard at http://<device>/ui/ saves Frigate's config as an attribute of the device in ThingsBoard.

docs.title: description: The five radar tables: detected object velocities, timed counts, raw speed and magnitude readings, and per-object summaries.
Radar
docs.text:
The OmniPreSense OPS243-A Doppler radar measures the speed and direction of whatever moves in front of it, does its own signal processing, and reports readings over USB as JSON. The Traffic Monitor turns on several of the radar's reporting modes when the service starts and whenever config.yml is saved, and stores each kind of reading in its own table. The radar's API guide describes the modes and the commands.

Reading Radar command Table What it is Detected object velocity ON radar_dov The radar decides an object is present when it sees two consecutive speed reports, then reports the highest speed, and again if a higher one follows. One or a few readings per object. These readings supply the speeds for events. Timed speed counts @O, every 300 seconds radar_timed_speed_counts How many objects passed in each direction during the interval, and their average speed Raw speed and magnitude OS and OM with O3 radar_raw_speed_magnitude The three strongest speed and magnitude pairs from each sample. Magnitude reflects the object's size, distance, and reflectivity. Strongest reading the first of the three above radar_raw_speed_magnitude_single The single strongest pair from each sample, for easier analysis Object summary OC radar_oc_payload One row per object, with its time in view, speed range, magnitude, and estimated length. Needs OPS9243 firmware.

Across the tables, direction is inbound (toward the radar) or outbound (away from it), speeds are positive for inbound and negative for outbound, and the unit is the radar's speed unit, mph by default. radarName is the radar's name from config.yml, and deployment_id points at the deployment the reading was taken in.
