docs.title: Contributing
docs.text:
Thank you for your interest in getting involved! We welcome all skill levels and abilities as contributions. Visit our Traffic Monitor GitHub page to get involved.

Contributions can include any of the following plus more!

  • 💡 Feature requests and use case ideas
  • 🐞 Bug reports
  • 👩‍💻 Code contributions, see Contributing
  • 👍 Comment on or thumbs-up milestones or issues
  • 💬 Questions, comments, and videos/images of your deployments on our Traffic Monitor Zulip Chat!

We foster a safe and welcoming community, review our Code of Conduct.

docs.title: Use of AI tools
docs.text: You may use AI coding assistants to help draft, review, or explain a contribution, but you remain its author: understand and test every change you submit. Never share images, video clips, or plate reads with an AI tool, and use placeholders instead of real passwords, keys, or tokens. The de-identified tmdb.sqlite database may be shared only with the device operator's explicit consent, and never if plate recognition was ever enabled, because it then holds plate numbers. See Use of AI tools in CONTRIBUTING.md for the details and for how to label AI-assisted commits.

docs.title: Writing docs
docs.text:
These docs are Markdown files in the repo's docs/ folder, built with Material for MkDocs. Docs changes go in the same pull request as the code they describe, against dev.

  • Preview while you edit: from the repo root, run python3 -m venv ~/.venvs/tm-docs && ~/.venvs/tm-docs/bin/pip install --require-hashes -r docs-site/requirements.txt once, then ~/.venvs/tm-docs/bin/mkdocs serve and open http://127.0.0.1:8000.
  • Check before you push: mkdocs build --strict fails on broken links, anchors, and images, and on pages missing from the nav. Pull requests run the same check.
  • New pages go in the nav: list in mkdocs.yml, under the section for the reader's job (see below). A page outside the folders already listed under the llmstxt plugin also goes in that plugin's matching section, so AI tools can find it in llms.txt. Keep a page's file path when you move it in the nav; if the path must change, add the old path to the moved map in docs-site/pages-root/404.html.
  • Images go in docs/assets/images/. Link them with Markdown, ![Alt text](../assets/images/name.png), so the build can check the path. Add a caption with <figure markdown="span"> (see existing pages).
  • Callouts use admonitions: !!! info, !!! success, !!! warning, or !!! danger, followed by the text indented four spaces.

Versions: pushes to dev publish to /dev/, and each release tag (vX.Y.Z) publishes a frozen copy and becomes /latest/, the default version.

docs.title: Style
docs.text:
Aim for pages that are complete but quick to read: everything the reader needs, and nothing they don't. These rules apply to every docs change, whether a person or an AI tool drafted it.

  • One reader and one job per page. Pages about installing, setup, configuration, the dashboards, and the data tell the person running a device what to do or what something means. Details for contributors go in the Development pages or in the README next to the code. Diátaxis names the four jobs: tutorial, how-to guide, reference, and explanation. Use it to decide what belongs on the page you're editing, not to reorganize the site. The nav sections map to those jobs:

    Section Job Reader Get started Explanation and orientation Anyone new Build your own, Deploy, Add-ons How-to guides, one task per page Someone building or installing a device Use the device How-to guides for the running device Someone operating a device Reference Tables: every setting, flag, topic, and column Someone looking a value up Ideas and use cases, Help Ideas, troubleshooting, and where to ask Someone curious or stuck Development Contributors You * Leave out what the reader won't act on, such as Ansible variables and task names, Node-RED node names, and files they won't open. Give real values, such as the default install folder /opt/traffic-monitor, instead of variables. * Revise in place. Rewrite the text your change affects and delete what it makes obsolete, rather than adding a paragraph. Keep the docs edit in proportion to the change; a diff that removes more than it adds is fine. * Describe how things work, not how they changed. Don't narrate changes ("now supports", "new in", "previously"). Each release has its own copy of the docs, and history belongs in commit messages and release notes. * Say each fact once, and link to it from other pages. Link to config files and code in the repo instead of copying them into a page, because copies go stale. Link to the main branch, which tracks the latest release, so the link matches /latest/ rather than /dev/. * Put the common case first. Move edge cases and troubleshooting into a collapsed callout (??? instead of !!!), a table, or the FAQ. * Use tables for reference data, with one row per setting or database column and its type, default, and meaning. * Keep the language plain: "you", present tense, active voice, short sentences, and no filler such as "simply", "just", or "note that". Save callouts for what the reader must not miss. * Check every value against the code, including defaults, paths, ports, and names.

For anything these rules don't cover, follow the Google developer documentation style guide.

docs.title: description: Set up to change the Traffic Monitor: the Node-RED flows, the database schema, and testing on a dev Pi.
Dev environment
docs.text:
The Traffic Monitor is open source, so you can change your devices to suit your needs. If others would benefit, join the community and contribute back.

The repository is a monorepo with everything needed to run a device: the installer, the container definitions, the Node-RED flows, and these docs.

docs.title: Node-RED logic
docs.text:
Node-RED runs the Traffic Monitor's logic: it receives events from Frigate and readings from the radar, pairs events with speeds, writes the database, serves the dashboards, and sends data on. The flows are in the repository at container/node-red-tm/data/flows.json, and the installer copies them to the device on every run, so changes made only in a device's editor are lost on the next update.

To develop on a device:

  1. Open the Node-RED editor at http://<device>/nr/ and log in as admin with password password.
  2. Create a new project and clone your fork of the repository. This replaces the flows on the device, so save any changes first.
  3. Point the project's flow and package files at container/node-red-tm/data/flows.json and package.json, so your edits land in the repository's files.
  4. Commit your changes to a branch of your fork.
  5. Open a pull request, following Contributing.

docs.title: Database schema
docs.text:
The tables are defined by numbered SQL migrations in container/node-red-tm/schema/migrations/, not by the flows. Each time node-red-tm.service starts, it applies the migrations the database doesn't have yet, before Node-RED opens it. The README.md in the schema directory describes the whole process, from writing a migration to testing the upgrade on a Pi.

To change the schema:

  1. Add the next numbered migration, regenerate schema.sql, and update the table docs under Data.

  2. Run the tests, using the dev environment from Contributing:

    .venv/bin/python -m pytest container/node-red-tm/schema/tests

To try a migration on a dev device, apply it while Node-RED is stopped. Deploying from the Node-RED editor doesn't restart the service, so it doesn't apply migrations. These commands use the default owner (tmadmin) and install folder, and run the migration script from your Node-RED project's clone:

sudo systemctl stop node-red-tm.service
sudo runuser -u tmadmin -- python3 \
    /opt/traffic-monitor/node-red-tm/data/projects/<project>/container/node-red-tm/schema/tmdb_migrate.py \
    --db /opt/traffic-monitor/node-red-tm/db/tmdb.sqlite
sudo systemctl start node-red-tm.service

The database records each migration it applies. If you change a migration after applying it, restore the copy saved in /opt/traffic-monitor/node-red-tm/db/backup/ and apply it again.

docs.title: Testing on a dev Pi
docs.text:
script/devpi/tmdev.py deploys your working copy to a bench Pi over SSH, runs commands on it, and records a PR's Pi test plan as a checklist. Every deploy, command, and check goes into a run log on your machine, so you can see later what ran on which Pi and how it went.

The Pis are defined in an inventory file that lists each Pi's address, login, and SSH key, plus the hardware it should have. That file and the run log stay on your machine, outside the repository. script/devpi/README.md covers setup and use.

Warning

Use these tools only with bench units, not field devices. Deploys pass -y to the installer, so the Pi reboots whenever the installer needs it.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text: A Traffic Monitor is a Raspberry Pi 5 running a few cooperating programs. Everything happens on the device, so it works without an internet connection once it's installed.

docs.title: From the street to the database
docs.text:
1. The camera streams H.265 video at 1536×864 and 10 frames per second to Frigate.
  2. Frigate finds and tracks objects in the video, using the AI accelerator if the device has one and the CPU if not. It records which zones each object passed through. When an object leaves the frame, Frigate publishes an event on the device's MQTT broker.
  3. The radar (optional) measures the speed and direction of whatever moves in front of it and reports readings over USB several times a second.

  4. Node-RED runs the Traffic Monitor logic. It keeps every radar reading, and it records every moving object from an enabled camera as an event. When the camera has a radar and the object entered any zone, it:

    • works out the direction of travel from the order in which the object entered zone_near and zone_far, or from the radar if the zones don't give one;
    • attaches a speed: the median radar reading in that direction while the object was in view, with a two-second margin on each side.

    Without a radar, events have no direction or speed. Direction and speed has the exact rules.

    The dashboards and the daily counts then filter the events by zone: they count objects that passed through zone_capture, and they use only objects that passed through zone_radar for speed statistics. 5. The database, one SQLite file on the device, stores the events, the radar readings, air quality readings from the optional sensor, and the device's deployment history. The dashboards read from it, and you can download it.

First-time setup walks through turning on detection and adjusting the four zones. Events lists every column an event has.

docs.title: What you see
docs.text: The device serves a home page at http://<device>/ that links to the dashboards, Frigate, and the system tools. Home page and apps describes each one.

docs.title: What stays on the device
docs.text: The database holds labels, times, speeds, and zones, not pictures. Frigate keeps cropped snapshots and short clips for about an hour so you can check what was detected, and nothing is sent anywhere unless you turn on an integration. Data and privacy has the details.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Three files on the device control the behavior described above. You edit them over SSH.

File What it controls Frigate's config.yml Camera, detection, zones, object filters, and recording. Most changes are made in Frigate's own web UI. See Tune object detection. Node-RED's config.yml Deployment location, which sensors are on, which radar pairs with which camera, and the ThingsBoard connection. Times shown on the dashboards use the device's time zone, which the installer sets. See config.yml settings. node-red-tm.env Radar serial ports, the database path, and the MQTT broker. See node-red-tm.env settings.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
The dashboard shows no counts

Follow the checklist in First-time setup. The usual causes, in order: detection is off in Frigate, the objects don't pass through zone_capture, or the camera isn't enabled in config.yml.

Counts, but no speeds

The radar must be enabled in config.yml and named in the camera's camera_radar, zone_radar must cover the road, and the device must be at a shallow angle to the traffic. If the radar was plugged in after the software was installed, rerun bash traffic-monitor/script/tmsetup.sh -t node-red-tm so the container can see it.

Frigate shows no camera image

Open Go2RTC Feeds from the home page. If the picam_h265_detect stream plays there, the camera and its stream work, and the fault is between Frigate and the stream. Either the camera is off in Frigate's configuration editor, where cameras: picam_h265: needs enabled: true, or Frigate's video decoding is failing, which shows as ffmpeg errors in the frigate.service log. If the stream doesn't play, check the camera cable, then look at the go2rtc_server.service log in System administration.

Detection is slow or misses objects

Without an AI accelerator, Frigate detects on the CPU and can't keep up with a busy road. Hardware lists the supported accelerators. If you added one after installing, see Add an accelerator later. With an accelerator, see Tune object detection.

The first install seems stuck

Building Frigate's container image compiles ffmpeg on the device, which takes about 20 minutes with little output. Leave it running. The whole first install takes 30 minutes or more.

A database download fails

See Data export.

I edited config.yml and nothing changed

The Traffic Monitor reads the file again when you save it, so a change that doesn't take effect usually means a YAML error, such as a wrong indent or a missing space after a colon. The node-red-tm.service log in System administration shows the error. Fix the file before you restart the service; config.yml settings explains why.

docs.title: What does the device record?
docs.text: The database records what passed (a label such as car), when, how fast, and through which zones. It holds no images and no plate numbers with the default settings. Frigate keeps a cropped snapshot and a short clip of each detection for about an hour, so you can check what it saw, and you can turn that off. By default, the device sends no images or video anywhere: everything is processed on the device, and the database holds only metadata. Anyone on your network can still see the live view, the recordings, and Frigate's snapshots, because none of them has a login. Data and privacy explains, and lists the features that would change what's stored.

docs.title: Why this design?
docs.text:
The Traffic Monitor is built privacy-first because we believe in:

  • Ethical and transparent monitoring. The code, the architecture, and the models are open, so anyone can see what the device does, and operators, especially public bodies, can be held to account.
  • Community safety and trust. Detection runs on the device, nothing is sent to an outside server unless you set it up, and the data stays in your control.
  • Unbiased data collection. Detection runs without human bias, but machine learning models can carry algorithmic bias. We use public-domain and open source models wherever possible and name the models in use.

To keep an area out of view, aim the camera so the area is out of frame. A motion mask doesn't hide it; see Data and privacy.

docs.title: How many objects can it track at once?
docs.text:
More than a busy street produces. The practical limit is objects hiding each other, as at the start of a race, where the camera can't see the person behind another.

The AI accelerator runs an inference in about 10 ms, which is about 100 inferences per second, and Frigate runs several inferences per frame when there's motion in several places. On a road with trees casting moving shadows, Frigate has been seen checking more than 18 motion regions and tracking 9 labeled objects at once, with inference time still around 9 ms. The video is decoded in hardware, and the CPU, which encodes the camera stream and runs motion detection, had headroom to spare. Frigate's discussions #7491 and #18326 explain how detections per frame are bounded.

A road where shadows produce many motion regions, all checked for objects

docs.title: Ideas and use cases
docs.text: The device collects more than counts. With extra zones in Frigate and the event data, you can study how people and vehicles interact. Two examples follow; share yours in Show and tell.

docs.title: Near misses at a crosswalk
docs.text:
A near miss is a driver and a vulnerable road user, such as a pedestrian at a crosswalk, in conflict at the same moment. These events are rarely captured today. The first step is a definition, and traffic law supplies one. As an example, Oregon's rules, summarized by Portland Bicycle School:

  • Every corner is a crosswalk (ORS 801.220).
  • A pedestrian has claimed the crossing as soon as any part of them, or their cane, wheelchair, or bicycle, enters it (ORS 811.028(4), 814.040(1)(a)).
  • A driver must stay stopped until the pedestrian has cleared the driver's lane, or the lane they're turning into, plus one more lane (ORS 811.028).

To capture conflicts:

  1. Mount the device with a view of the whole intersection.
  2. Draw zones for the pedestrian areas and the driver areas.
  3. Each person and car event then records its start_time, end_time, and entered_zones.
  4. Download the data and look for a car entering a driver zone while a person was in the conflicting pedestrian zone.

For example, a person in zone_ped_ne about to cross south or west, and a car that enters zone_intersection_e and turns into zone_intersection_n before the person has crossed, is a near miss or at least an illegal turn. You can tighten the definition further: was the car stationary at the stop sign first, or did a pedestrian zone at the very edge of the sidewalk show intent to cross? A person and a car in the same road zone at the same time is the most serious case.

Zones for a near-miss study: pedestrian zones on each corner and intersection zones on each approach

docs.title: Vehicles that don't stop at a stop sign
docs.text:
A rolling stop, also called a California stop or Rhode Island stop, is a vehicle that passes a stop sign without stopping fully or for the required time. Some places let cyclists treat a stop sign as a yield (the Idaho stop).

  1. Mount the device high, looking down at the whole intersection.

  2. In Frigate, draw a thin stop-sign zone across the road just before each stop sign, such as zone_stop_sign_e and zone_stop_sign_w for a two-way stop.

  3. Give each stop-sign zone a loitering time that matches your jurisdiction, such as 3 seconds, and limit it to car if you like. The zone then appears in an event's entered_zones only if the vehicle stayed in it that long. A vehicle that rolled through has an event without the zone.

  4. Optionally add wider zones for each approach, so you can also see turning movements: a car that went from zone_intersection_e to zone_intersection_n turned right.

  5. Check the zones against a few real vehicles in Frigate's Explore view. It can take a while to find a car that stops properly.

docs.title: description: Where to ask questions, report bugs, and share ideas: the chat, GitHub discussions, and issues.
Get support
docs.text: The Traffic Monitor is a volunteer-run open source project. The community answers questions as it can, so please be patient, and help others when you can. Everyone follows the Code of Conduct.

docs.title: Search first
docs.text: Search these docs, then the repository: the search box at the top right covers discussions, issues, and code, with filters on the left.

docs.title: Chat
docs.text: The Traffic Monitor Zulip chat is the quickest place to ask a question, suggest an idea, or show a deployment. Developers discuss code there too, so it's also the place to start contributing.

docs.title: GitHub discussions
docs.text:
The discussions board is for longer conversations:

  • 💬 General: anything at all
  • 💡 Ideas: feature ideas, and votes on them
  • 🗳️ Polls
  • 🙏 Q&A: ask for help
  • 👐 Show and tell: what you've built

docs.title: GitHub issues
docs.text:
Open an issue for a specific bug, a feature request, or a technical question that the discussions haven't answered. Include enough detail for someone else to reproduce or understand it.

  • 🐞 Bug report
  • 💡 Feature request

An issue may be closed without a full resolution, for example as a duplicate, after inactivity, or because the work is tracked elsewhere. That isn't a lack of interest; comment or reopen if it still matters.

docs.title: Network ports
docs.text:
Other computers reach the Traffic Monitor's apps through the home page on port 80. The apps themselves accept connections only from the device.

Port Used for 22 SSH 80 The home page and every app it links to 1883 MQTT, only when the broker has a login. See MQTT and ThingsBoard. 5353 (UDP) <hostname>.local names (mDNS) 8554 The camera stream (RTSP), with a username and password 9090 Cockpit, with your Raspberry Pi login. Use it if the home page doesn't load.

When the device hosts its own Wi-Fi network, it also answers DHCP and DNS on it.

docs.title: Camera stream login
docs.text:
The camera stream on port 8554 needs the username frigate and a password generated on the device at install. To play the stream in another program, such as VLC, read the password on the device:

sudo cat /etc/traffic-monitor/secrets/go2rtc_rtsp_password

Then open rtsp://frigate:<password>@<device>:8554/picam_h265_detect.

docs.title: Installer options
docs.text:
script/tmsetup.sh in the repository installs and updates the Traffic Monitor. Run it from the device, or from another computer with -H. Install the software and Update the software show the usual runs.

bash traffic-monitor/script/tmsetup.sh [flags]

docs.title: Flags
docs.text:
Flag Meaning -h Show the usage text and exit. -y Answer yes to every prompt, including the reboot. -v Verbose output. Repeat for more. -f Replace the user-editable settings files with fresh copies from the templates. See What -f replaces. -t TAG Run one component, plus anything that has to change with it. Repeat for several. See Tags. -T List the tags and exit. -C NAME[,NAME] Turn on an optional component: plate_recognizer (see Plate Recognizer), or mqtt_lan, which creates an MQTT broker login when there isn't one (see Connect from other devices). -u Also upgrade the operating system's packages (apt full-upgrade). -d PATH Install folder. Default /opt/traffic-monitor. The docs assume the default. -o USER Owner of the installed files and processes. Default tmadmin, created by the installer. -g GROUP Group of the installed files. Default tmadmin. -z TIMEZONE Time zone for the system and the dashboards, as a tz database name. Default America/Los_Angeles. -L PATH Where to write the installer's log. -a ARG Pass an extra argument to the underlying Ansible run, without its leading hyphen.

Remote runs:

Flag Meaning -H HOST[,HOST] Install to these devices over SSH instead of the local machine. Separate several with commas. -l USER The SSH username on the devices. -k Ask for the SSH password. -K Ask for the password for administrator rights (sudo). Needed on Raspberry Pi OS unless you've set up passwordless sudo.

docs.title: Tags
docs.text:
Each tag reruns one part of the install. Without -t, everything runs. The pod and the reverse proxy have to change together, so the podman, frigate, node-red-tm, go2rtc, and revproxy tags each update both.

Tag What it does base Operating system packages, the owner account, and Cockpit. It runs with every -t. full_upgrade The apt full-upgrade, when -u is given wifi Wi-Fi setup go2rtc The camera streaming service on the host, and the stream login Frigate uses to read it detectors Detects the Coral or Hailo accelerator, installs its driver, and writes the boot configuration. See Add an accelerator later. podman The container runtime and the pod frigate Frigate's container, settings, and the devices it needs node-red-tm Node-RED's container, flows, settings, and the radars it needs. Rerun it after plugging in a radar. plate-recognizer The optional Plate Recognizer container revproxy The home page and reverse proxy tm-control Installs the tm-control command, which updates settings files from earlier versions. The frigate and go2rtc tags install it too and run it to give Frigate's config.yml the stream login.

docs.title: What -f replaces
docs.text:
Every run replaces the container images, service units, Node-RED flows, and the reverse proxy configuration. These files are kept unless you pass -f:

  • /opt/traffic-monitor/node-red-tm/config/config.yml
  • /opt/traffic-monitor/node-red-tm/node-red-tm.env
  • /opt/traffic-monitor/frigate/config/config.yml, which holds zones and masks drawn in Frigate
  • /opt/traffic-monitor/frigate/frigate.env
  • /opt/traffic-monitor/plate-recognizer/plate-recognizer.env, if Plate Recognizer is installed

With -f, each is replaced by a fresh copy from its template, and the old file stays next to it with a timestamp in its name so you can copy your settings back. The MQTT broker login carries into the fresh node-red-tm.env and frigate.env. A fresh Frigate config has detection off and the sample zones, so afterwards turn detection on and redo your zones and masks, as in First-time setup.

docs.title: Add an accelerator later
docs.text:
After you add or change a Coral or Hailo accelerator, rerun two tags and reboot when the installer asks:

bash traffic-monitor/script/tmsetup.sh -t detectors -t frigate

That installs the driver and gives Frigate's container the device. Frigate's own config.yml still names the old detector, because the installer writes its detectors: and model: sections only when it creates the file. Either edit those two sections by hand to match the template, or add -f to the command above and then redo your Frigate settings, as What -f replaces describes.

docs.title: Reboots
docs.text: The installer edits the boot configuration and installs kernel drivers, so it asks to reboot when needed. On the device, it prompts, and with -y it doesn't ask. Either way the reboot starts one minute later. Remote devices reboot by themselves. Services stay stopped until the reboot.

docs.title: description: The Data export dashboard: download the database or a JSON export, and add comments for whoever analyzes the data.
Data export
docs.text:
Open http://<device>/dashboard/database, or Database in the dashboard's sidebar. This page gets data off the device and lets you leave notes in it.

The Data export page

docs.title: Comments
docs.text: A comment is a timestamped note stored in the comments table, for whoever analyzes the data later: a settings change, road work, an event in the area. Give it an effective date and an optional expiry date, the text, and your name; only the name is required. The form also has time fields, but only the dates are kept. Without an effective date, the comment takes effect when you save it. Data and privacy lists the columns.

docs.title: Download the database
docs.text:
Downloads the whole database as a compressed archive named <hostname>_<time>_tmdb.tar.gz. The page shows the database's size in megabytes. The device first makes a consistent copy of the database, so a large one can take a minute or two before the download starts. The copy needs free space about the size of the database; if there isn't enough, the page says so. A 3 GB file can then take about 5 minutes to compress and several more to download. Cancel also works while the copy is being made: the download stops once the copy is done, and no archive is sent. If a download fails, you see the reason instead of a broken file.

Unpack the archive with tar -xvzf on Linux or Mac, or with 7-Zip on Windows. Inside is tmdb.sqlite, which opens in DB Browser for SQLite or any SQLite library.

docs.title: Download JSON
docs.text:
Exports part of the data as JSON files in a compressed archive named <hostname>_<time>_json.tar.gz. Choose what to export and a start and end time, which default to the last 7 days:

Choice Contents Everything The events table, the five radar tables, and the airquality table All event types The whole events table for the time range One object type, such as car or person The events of that type Air quality The airquality table Radar The radar tables

The files are plain JSON, readable in any text editor or loaded straight into a notebook.

docs.title: description: The Monitoring dashboard: today's counts, car speed statistics, hourly and daily charts, and the latest events with their radar readings.
Monitoring
docs.text:
Open http://<device>/dashboard/monitoring, or open Dashboard from the home page and choose Monitoring in the sidebar. Monitoring shows the counts and speed statistics for one camera and one radar at a time.

The Monitoring page, numbered as in the list below
  1. Sensor selection. A radar and a camera picker, listing every sensor in config.yml, enabled or not. The counts and statistics on this page follow the camera and radar selected on the legacy dashboard at http://<device>/ui/, not the selection here. On a device with one camera and one radar, they're the same.

  2. Car speed statistics for the current day, which starts at 04:00 local time. They cover car events that passed through both zone_capture and zone_radar and got a speed from the radar. Speeds are absolute values, so inbound and outbound are pooled, and every value is rounded to a whole number.

    The percentiles come from sorting the day's cars by speed and splitting them into 20 groups of equal size, so they're approximate. With few cars, some stay empty: the 25th percentile needs 5 cars, the median 10, the 75th percentile and iqr_upper 15, and the 85th percentile 17.

    Statistic Meaning count Cars with a speed mean_speed Average speed p25_speed, p50_speed, p75_speed, p85_speed 25th, 50th (median), 75th, and 85th percentile speeds. The 85th percentile is the usual basis for speed limits. max_speed Fastest car count_over_25 Cars faster than 25, in the radar's units iqr_upper The outlier line: p75_speed plus 1.5 times the interquartile range iqr_upper_freq Cars faster than iqr_upper, the outliers

  3. Today's counts by object type for events that passed through zone_capture. The day starts at 04:00 local time, so from midnight until 04:00 these counts and the speed statistics are empty. Objects that pass in those hours are left out of the day's counts, but they appear in the hourly and daily charts.

  4. Hourly counts by object type for the last 36 hours, for events that passed through zone_capture.
  5. Daily counts by object type for the last 10 calendar days, for events that passed through zone_capture.
  6. Latest observations. The 21 most recent events from any camera that passed through zone_radar, newest first, including events without a speed. Each card shows Frigate's thumbnail of the object, the direction, the speed, and the radar's raw readings from the start of the event to its end: how many there were ("radar hits"), the range of their magnitudes and speeds, and two charts, Radar Magnitude and Radar Speed. The charts show whether the readings came from one object or from several at once. They're the raw readings, not the ones the speed was worked out from. The list is kept in memory, so it empties when Node-RED restarts.

Counts and statistics come from the events table; see Events. The same counts are published over MQTT on tm/events; see MQTT and ThingsBoard.

docs.title: description: The Movements dashboard: counts of objects by the sequence of zones they passed through, for checking against manual counts.
Movements
docs.text:
Open http://<device>/dashboard/movements. Movements counts objects by the path they took through your zones, which is how you check the device against a manual count or confirm that the zones capture what you want.

Movements come from the entered_zones of each event, so they depend on how the zones are drawn.

The Movements page
  1. Zones. Tick the zones to include. The four standard zone_* zones are unticked by default, so that zones you drew for your own analysis stand out.
  2. Intermediate zones. Choose Show intermediate zones to count each full sequence of zones separately, or Show just initial & final zones to group by where an object entered and where it left.
  3. Time range. Start and end times; the last 7 days by default. In time zones east of UTC, or with a half-hour offset, the page shows no counts for any range.
  4. Counts by object type for each zone sequence that matches.

docs.text:

docs.title: description: The device's home page and the apps it links to: dashboards, Frigate, Node-RED, camera feeds, and Cockpit.
Home page and apps
docs.text:
Open http://<device>/ in a browser on the same network. <device> is the hostname you set when you imaged the card, followed by .local (for example http://tm-01.local/), or the device's IP address.

The home page links to every app on the device.

Link Path What it is Login Dashboard /dashboard/ The Traffic Monitor dashboards: Monitoring, Movements, and Data export, which opens first. Switch pages in the sidebar. None Frigate /frigate/ Object detection: live view, detections with snapshots and clips, zones, masks, and the Frigate settings. See Tune object detection. None Legacy Dashboard /ui/ The older dashboard, with the same counts and speed statistics as Monitoring. It's the only dashboard that shows air quality readings, and the Monitoring dashboard's counts follow its camera and radar selection. Its System Settings tab shows the device's name, time zone, and software versions, and holds the ThingsBoard Backup & Restore section. None Node-RED admin console /nr/ The flow editor, for developers. See Dev environment. admin / password Go2RTC Feeds /feeds/ The camera streams the Pi camera produces, for checking that the camera works. It's for watching only: go2rtc's settings, stream editor, and log pages aren't available here. None Cockpit-Project system administration /system/ Services, logs, containers, and a terminal. See System administration. Your Raspberry Pi user account Finding the device's address
  • If you set a hostname in Raspberry Pi Imager, http://<hostname>.local/ works from most computers and phones on the same network.
  • Otherwise, look the device up in your router's list of connected devices, or see Find the IP address of your Raspberry Pi.
  • A pre-built unit may host its own Wi-Fi network. Connect to it and use the hostname or the gateway address. Your provider's instructions take precedence.
If the home page doesn't load

The apps accept connections only from the device, so they have no address of their own on your network. Open Cockpit at http://<device>:9090, log in with your Raspberry Pi user account, and check the services as described in System administration. Network ports lists what the device opens.

docs.title: Cockpit
docs.text: Open http://<device>/system/ and log in with your Raspberry Pi user account. Cockpit shows the services and their logs, the Podman containers, system updates, and a terminal, so most administration needs no SSH client.

docs.title: Services
docs.text:
The Traffic Monitor runs as systemd services. The app containers run inside one Podman pod. nginx runs on the host network, outside the pod, so the home page stays up when the pod is down.

Service What it runs traffic-monitor.service The pod that holds Frigate, Node-RED, and Plate Recognizer if installed frigate.service Frigate, object detection node-red-tm.service Node-RED: the Traffic Monitor logic, dashboards, database, and MQTT broker revproxy.service nginx, which serves the home page and the /dashboard/, /frigate/, and other paths plate-recognizer.service The optional Plate Recognizer add-on go2rtc_server.service go2rtc, which reads the Pi camera and streams it to Frigate. It runs on the host, not in the pod.

Over SSH:

sudo systemctl status traffic-monitor.service   # or any service above
sudo systemctl restart node-red-tm.service      # after editing node-red-tm.env
sudo journalctl -u frigate.service -f           # follow a service's log
sudo podman ps                                  # running containers

docs.title: When to restart what
docs.text: After you Do this Edit Node-RED's config.yml Nothing. The Traffic Monitor reads the file again when you save it. If the change doesn't show, check the file for a YAML error. Edit node-red-tm.env sudo systemctl restart node-red-tm.service. The container reads the file only when it starts. Change the MQTT broker login in node-red-tm.env bash traffic-monitor/script/tmsetup.sh -t node-red-tm. A restart isn't enough; node-red-tm.env settings explains why. Change Frigate's config in its UI Choose Save & Restart in Frigate's config editor, or restart frigate.service. Plug in a radar Rerun the installer for Node-RED so the radar is passed to the container: bash traffic-monitor/script/tmsetup.sh -t node-red-tm. Add or change an AI accelerator Rerun the installer with -t detectors -t frigate, then update Frigate's detector settings. See Add an accelerator later. Move the device to a new site Follow First-time setup again: adjust the zones and update the location.

docs.title: Where things are
docs.text:
Everything the installer manages lives under /opt/traffic-monitor/.

Path Contents node-red-tm/config/config.yml Traffic Monitor settings. See config.yml settings. node-red-tm/node-red-tm.env Radar ports, database path, MQTT broker. See node-red-tm.env settings. node-red-tm/db/tmdb.sqlite The database. db/backup/ holds the copy saved before the most recent schema change. frigate/config/config.yml Frigate's settings, including zones and masks. frigate/storage/ Frigate's snapshots and recordings. plate-recognizer/plate-recognizer.env Plate Recognizer credentials, if the add-on is installed.
